awd_titl_txt: Travel Grant: Expanding Opportunities for Faculty at Non-R1 Primarily Undergraduate Institutions
awd_abstract_narration:
The American Geophysical Union’s Fall Meeting is the country’s largest gathering of geoscientists.  The conference provides networking and learning opportunities, but has relatively few attendees from primarily undergraduate institutions and community colleges.  This award provides travel support for attendees from institutions that do not have significant resources available to provide travel funding.  

The 2025 American Geophysical Union meeting will take place from 15-19 December in New Orleans, LA.  This award will provide a travel stipend for roughly 40 participants attending the conference.  The cohort of participants will be selected to ensure representation from 2- and 4-year colleges that are deemed primarily undergraduate institutions and consist of a mix of early- and mid-career faculty.  In addition to attending the meeting, the participants will participate in pre-meeting cohort building exercises, participate in professional development activities, and review student posters.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
The American Geophysical Union (AGU) Faculty Travel Grant program helped college professors who teach geoscience attend the AGU Annual Meeting, one of the world’s largest Earth and space science conferences. Many faculty at community colleges and primarily undergraduate colleges do not have the funding to attend conferences like this, even though they play an important role in educating the next generation of scientists. By providing travel support, this program gave these faculty members the opportunity to learn about the latest scientific discoveries, connect with other researchers, and bring new ideas back to their students and campuses.

In 2025, the program selected 41 faculty members from community colleges and primarily undergraduate institutions across the United States. 40 faculty participated in person at the conference, many of whom would not have been able to attend without this support. Before the meeting, participants joined an online orientation where they learned how to make the most of the conference, met one another, and received guidance from faculty who had participated in the program the previous year. A WhatsApp group and cohort activities helped participants build a supportive professional community before they even arrived.

At the conference, faculty attended scientific presentations, workshops, keynote lectures, and networking events that expanded their knowledge and introduced them to new research, teaching ideas, and collaborators. Nearly two-thirds of the participants also shared their own work by presenting research or leading scientific sessions. Together, the group explored ways to strengthen undergraduate geoscience education, including discussing the creation of a new AGU working group focused on undergraduate education. Participants also encouraged the younger scientists by providing feedback to high school students presenting research through the AGU Bright STaRS program.

The impact of the program extends well beyond a single conference. Faculty returned to their classrooms with new scientific knowledge, stronger professional networks, and fresh ideas for teaching and mentoring students. New collaborations formed during the meeting are expected to lead to future research projects and funding opportunities. By investing in faculty who teach at institutions that educate thousands of undergraduate students each year, the program multiplied its impact, improving science education, expanding research opportunities for students, and strengthening the future geoscience workforce.

Overall, the AGU Faculty Travel Grant program demonstrated that removing financial barriers to professional development can have lasting benefits for faculty, students, and the broader scientific community. By investing in faculty at community colleges and PUIs, the project helped strengthen research capacity, improve science education, and expand the network of scientists working to address important challenges related to the Earth and environment.
